nameStory: The American Angle Shades gets its name from the distinctive angular, slanted markings across its forewings that create shadowy patterns reminiscent of architectural angles and shadows. The "American" part distinguishes it from a similar European species called simply "Angle Shades," showing how moth enthusiasts noticed the family resemblance across continents.
description: The American Angle Shades is a medium-sized moth in the cutworm family, with forewings that typically span about 1.5-2 inches across. Its most striking feature is the angular, zigzag pattern of dark and light bands that sweep across its wings like abstract brushstrokes. The moth has a sturdy, somewhat chunky build typical of noctuids, with feathery antennae and wings that fold in a tent-like shape when at rest. Like other cutworm moths, it's primarily active at night and often attracted to outdoor lights.

idTips.label: Angular wing pattern
idTips.description: Look for distinctive zigzag or chevron-shaped dark markings that cut across the forewings at sharp angles, creating a geometric shadow effect that's unmistakable

idTips.label: Wing texture and color
idTips.description: Forewings feel smooth to the touch and display muted browns, grays, and sometimes purplish tones with a subtle sheen that catches light differently than the duller cutworm moths

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: When at rest, wings fold in a steep triangular tent over the body, with the angular patterns creating an almost architectural silhouette against tree bark or walls

idTips.label: Body build
idTips.description: Medium-sized with a robust, fuzzy thorax that feels dense and woolly if gently touched, distinguishing it from more delicate moth families

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with the characteristic heavy, somewhat erratic flight of cutworm moths, often spiraling around lights rather than the straight-line flight of some other night moths

habitat: American Angle Shades can be found throughout New England's mixed and deciduous forests, particularly in areas with oak, maple, and other hardwood trees where their caterpillars feed. They're commonly encountered around porch lights, outdoor fixtures, and lit windows in both rural and suburban areas near wooded habitats. Look for them in forest edges, parks with mature trees, and wooded residential neighborhoods from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, becoming active as temperatures warm. This is when you're most likely to spot fresh individuals with crisp, unworn wing patterns at outdoor lights.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most abundant and actively mating. Moths are frequently seen at lights during warm summer evenings, and their distinctive angular patterns are easiest to observe.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, though individuals may appear more worn and faded. Late-season moths often have slightly tattered wing edges from their active summer lives.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active during winter months. The species overwinters in earlier life stages, so no moths will be visible until the following spring emergence.

funFact: Despite being called "cutworm moths," many species in this family, including the American Angle Shades, don't actually cut plants as caterpillars - the name comes from just a few notorious species in the family whose larvae do cut down garden plants at soil level, giving the entire family of over 11,000 species worldwide a somewhat unfair reputation!
confusionNotes: The angular wing patterns are so distinctive that American Angle Shades is rarely confused with other moths once you know what to look for. The key memory trick is "angles and shades" - if you see sharp, geometric dark markings creating shadow-like patterns, you've likely found your angle shades rather than the more rounded or wavy patterns of other noctuids.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name Euplexia benesimilis has an interesting backstory - "benesimilis" means "quite similar" in Latin, likely referring to its resemblance to the European Angle Shades moth, showing how early moth taxonomists recognized the close relationship between these transatlantic cousins.
compareHints: Since American Angle Shades is the only Euplexia species in New England, compare it with other cutworm moths in the Noctuidae family. Most other noctuids have rounded kidney-shaped spots or wavy lines on their wings, while American Angle Shades stands out with its sharp, geometric angular markings. The angular pattern is more pronounced and architectural-looking than the softer, curved patterns typical of most cutworm moth relatives.
